Azure Services and Third-Party Integration — Service Bus, Event Grid, API Management

2024-03-28 Azure Integration Azure Developer Associate

Azure provides a rich set of messaging and integration services that connect applications, services, and third-party systems. For the Developer Associate exam the focus is on knowing which service to use for which scenario — and understanding the key properties of each one.

Azure Service Bus

Service Bus is a fully managed enterprise message broker for reliable, asynchronous communication between decoupled services. It supports both queues (point-to-point) and topics (publish/subscribe).

Queues vs topics

  • Queue — a single consumer receives each message (FIFO with sessions, competing consumers without)
  • Topic — messages are published to a topic and delivered to one or more subscriptions; each subscription acts as an independent queue
  • Subscriptions can have filters (SQL-like or correlation) to receive only matching messages

Key features

  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ) — messages that fail processing or expire move to the DLQ for inspection and retry
  • Message sessions — guarantee ordered delivery and group related messages; required for FIFO processing
  • Duplicate detection — automatically discards duplicate messages within a configurable time window
  • Message lock — a receiver holds a lock on the message while processing; if the lock expires, the message becomes available again
  • Message size up to 256 KB (Standard tier) or 100 MB (Premium tier)
  • Premium tier supports VNet integration, private endpoints, and message encryption

When to use Service Bus vs Storage Queue

  • Use Service Bus when you need guaranteed delivery, ordering, sessions, dead-lettering, or messages larger than 64 KB
  • Use Storage Queue for simple, high-volume workloads where those guarantees are not required

Azure Event Grid

Event Grid is a fully managed event routing service built on a publish/subscribe model. It routes discrete events from sources to handlers, with filtering and fan-out support.

Core concepts

  • Event source — emits events (Azure Blob Storage, Resource Groups, custom topics, etc.)
  • Topic — the endpoint where events are published; system topics are created automatically for Azure services
  • Event subscription — defines which events to receive and where to deliver them
  • Event handler — receives and processes events (Azure Functions, Logic Apps, Service Bus, Event Hubs, Webhooks, etc.)

Key properties

  • Near real-time event delivery with at-least-once delivery guarantee
  • Built-in retry with exponential backoff (up to 24 hours)
  • Event filtering by event type and subject prefix/suffix — reduces unnecessary invocations
  • Events are discrete notifications (something happened) — not large payloads; max 1 MB per event
  • Dead-lettering supported: undeliverable events go to a storage container you specify

Event Grid vs Service Bus

  • Use Event Grid for reactive, event-driven architectures where many subscribers need to react to the same event
  • Use Service Bus for reliable message processing workflows where order, sessions, or transactional guarantees matter

Azure Event Hubs

Event Hubs is a big-data streaming platform and event ingestion service. It is designed for high-throughput telemetry and log ingestion from many producers.

Key concepts

  • Partition — events are written to partitions; consumers read from specific partitions independently
  • Consumer group — a view of the event stream; multiple consumer groups can read the same data independently without interfering
  • Capture — automatically stores raw events to Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage for batch processing
  • Retention is configurable from 1 to 90 days (Standard and Premium tiers)
  • Throughput measured in throughput units (Standard) or processing units (Premium)

When to use Event Hubs

  • Telemetry ingestion (IoT devices, application logs, click streams)
  • When you need multiple independent consumers to read the same stream
  • When downstream processing is done by Spark, Stream Analytics, or Azure Functions with the Event Hub trigger

Azure API Management (APIM)

API Management is a fully managed API gateway that sits in front of your backend services. It handles cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, caching, and transformation.

Core components

  • API Gateway — the runtime proxy that accepts requests, applies policies, and forwards calls to backends
  • Developer portal — auto-generated documentation and a self-service portal for API consumers
  • Management plane — the Azure portal, REST API, or Bicep/Terraform used to configure APIM

Policies

Policies are the main extensibility mechanism in APIM. They are XML-based rules applied at four lifecycle points: inbound (on the request before it hits the backend), backend (just before the backend call), outbound (on the response before it reaches the caller), and on-error.

  • rate-limit-by-key / quota-by-key — throttle requests per subscription or IP
  • validate-jwt — enforce Entra ID or other JWT tokens before passing to the backend
  • set-header / rewrite-uri — transform requests and responses
  • cache-lookup / cache-store — cache backend responses
  • mock-response — return a static response without calling the backend; useful for testing

Subscriptions and products

  • APIs are grouped into products (e.g. "Free tier", "Premium"); consumers subscribe to a product
  • Each subscription gets a key that must be sent in the Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key header by default
  • Subscriptions can be scoped to a product, a single API, or all APIs

Azure Logic Apps

Logic Apps is a low-code integration platform for automating workflows that connect Azure services, SaaS applications, and on-premises systems.

  • Workflows are defined visually or in JSON; no code required for most scenarios
  • Over 400 built-in connectors (Office 365, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Twitter, etc.)
  • Standard tier (single-tenant) runs on App Service Infrastructure — supports VNet integration and stateful/stateless workflows
  • Consumption tier — serverless, multi-tenant, pay-per-execution
  • Prefer Logic Apps over custom code for orchestrating SaaS integrations where connectors already exist; use Azure Functions for custom logic that doesn't map to a connector

Integrating Third-Party Services

Webhooks

  • Many third-party services push events to a URL you provide — validate the payload signature before processing
  • Azure Functions with an HTTP trigger is a common handler for incoming webhooks
  • Use Event Grid to fan out webhook events to multiple internal handlers

Outbound HTTP calls from Azure Functions

  • Use HttpClient (injected as a singleton) or the SDK of the third-party service
  • Store API keys in Key Vault and access them via Key Vault references or SecretClient
  • Use Polly or the built-in retry policies in Durable Functions for transient failures

SendGrid (email)

  • Azure Functions has a SendGrid output binding — declare it in the binding config, pass the message object, no HTTP client code needed
  • The API key is stored in app settings and referenced by binding attribute name

Twilio (SMS)

  • Azure Functions has a Twilio output binding for sending SMS from a function output
  • Same pattern: binding config declares the connection, function code returns the message body

Service selection cheat sheet

  • Reliable ordered processing → Service Bus (queues with sessions)
  • Pub/sub fan-out to multiple subscribers → Service Bus topics or Event Grid
  • High-throughput event streaming / telemetry → Event Hubs
  • Reactive events from Azure resources → Event Grid (system topics)
  • API gateway / throttling / auth enforcement → API Management
  • SaaS workflow automation → Logic Apps
  • Custom compute / code → Azure Functions
